questions.question: For the linear program (P) $\max\{\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b},\ \boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ and its dual (D) $\min\{\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\colon\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{c},\ \boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$, which statement is the weak duality theorem?
options: $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}$ for every $\boldsymbol{x}$ with $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}$ and every $\boldsymbol{y}$ with $\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{c}$, signs unrestricted.
$\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}$ for every feasible solution $\boldsymbol{x}$ of (P), but only for an optimal solution $\boldsymbol{y}$ of (D).
$\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}$ for every feasible solution $\boldsymbol{x}$ of (P) and every feasible solution $\boldsymbol{y}$ of (D).
$\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}$ for all feasible $\boldsymbol{x}$ and $\boldsymbol{y}$, so each dual value is a lower bound for (P).

questions.question: For (P) $\max\{\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b},\ \boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ and its dual (D) $\min\{\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\colon\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{c},\ \boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$, which conditions justify the first step $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}$ of the proof of weak duality?
options: The dual constraint $\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{c}$, weighted componentwise by $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$.
The primal constraint $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}$, weighted componentwise by $\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$.
The dual constraint $\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{c}$, together with the sign condition $\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$.
The primal constraint $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}$, together with the sign condition $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$.

questions.question: Feasible solutions $\boldsymbol{x}^{\ast}$ of (P) $\max\{\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b},\ \boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ and $\boldsymbol{y}^{\ast}$ of its dual (D) $\min\{\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\colon\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{c},\ \boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ satisfy $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}^{\ast}=\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}^{\ast}$. What follows by weak duality?
options: $\boldsymbol{x}^{\ast}$ is optimal for (P), but $\boldsymbol{y}^{\ast}$ need not be an optimal solution of (D).
Nothing yet: two feasible solutions that are not optimal can also have equal values.
$\boldsymbol{x}^{\ast}$ is optimal for (P), and no other feasible solution of (P) is optimal.
$\boldsymbol{x}^{\ast}$ is optimal for (P) and $\boldsymbol{y}^{\ast}$ is optimal for (D), with equal values.

questions.question: The linear program (P) $\max\{\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b},\ \boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ is unbounded. What does weak duality imply for its dual (D) $\min\{\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\colon\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{c},\ \boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$?
options: (D) is unbounded as well, its objective values going to $-\infty$.
(D) has no feasible solution, so it has no optimal value at all.
(D) has an optimal solution, and its optimal value equals $0$.
(D) has an optimal value that exceeds every value of (P).

questions.question: A firm solves (P) $\max\{\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b},\ \boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ with capacities $b_i$, unit profits $c_j$ and use $a_{i,j}$ of resource $i$ per unit of product $j$. A buyer offers prices $\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$ per unit of resource with $\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{c}$. What does weak duality say?
options: The payment $\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}$ for all capacity equals the firm's largest possible profit.
Each offered price $y_i$ is at least the unit profit $c_j$ of each product $j$.
The payment $\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}$ for all capacity is at least the profit $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ of any feasible plan $\boldsymbol{x}$.
The payment $\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}$ for all capacity is at most the profit $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ of any feasible plan $\boldsymbol{x}$.

questions.question: For $\max Z=5x_1+4x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\leq7$, $2x_1+x_2\leq10$, $x_1+3x_2\leq15$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, the point $\boldsymbol{x}=(2,4)$ is feasible, and $\boldsymbol{y}=(2,2,0)$ is feasible for the dual $\min W=7y_1+10y_2+15y_3$ subject to $y_1+2y_2+y_3\geq5$, $y_1+y_2+3y_3\geq4$, $\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$. What do these two points give for the optimal value $Z^{\ast}$?
options: $Z^{\ast}\leq26$
$26\leq Z^{\ast}\leq34$
$Z^{\ast}\geq34$

questions.question: For $\max Z=3x_1+2x_2+x_3$ subject to $x_1+x_2+x_3\leq8$, $2x_1+x_3\leq6$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, with dual $\min W=8y_1+6y_2$ subject to $y_1+2y_2\geq3$, $y_1\geq2$, $y_1+y_2\geq1$, $\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, the point $\boldsymbol{x}=(1,5,2)$ is feasible. What does it give for the optimal value $W^{\ast}$ of the dual?
options: $W^{\ast}\leq15$
No bound on $W^{\ast}$ until $\boldsymbol{x}$ is known to be optimal
$W^{\ast}\geq15$

questions.question: For (P) $\max Z=x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\leq2$, $-x_1-x_2\leq-3$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, the dual (D) is $\min W=2y_1-3y_2$ subject to $y_1-y_2\geq1$, $y_1-y_2\geq1$, $\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$. For every $t\geq0$, $\boldsymbol{y}=(1+t,t)$ is feasible for (D) with $W=2-t$. What does weak duality give for (P)?
options: (P) has no feasible solution: its feasible region is empty.
(P) is unbounded, its objective values going to $+\infty$.
(P) has an optimal solution, with value at most $2$ by the point $t=0$.
Nothing follows, since the bound needs an optimal $\boldsymbol{y}$ of (D).

questions.question: For $\max Z=4x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\leq5$, $2x_1-x_2\leq4$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, take the feasible $\boldsymbol{x}=(2,1)$ and the dual feasible $\boldsymbol{y}=(3,1)$. Which values does the chain $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\leq\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}$ take?
options: $9\leq14\leq19$
$9\leq13\leq19$
$9\leq12\leq19$
$9\leq15\leq19$

questions.question: For $\max Z=3x_1+2x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\leq6$, $x_1+3x_2\leq12$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, the vector $\boldsymbol{y}=(2,1)$ is feasible for the dual ($y_1+y_2\geq3$, $y_1+3y_2\geq2$, $\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$). Comparing objective values only, which proposed point can be rejected as infeasible for the primal by weak duality?
options: $\boldsymbol{x}=(6,0)$
$\boldsymbol{x}=(7,2)$
$\boldsymbol{x}=(8,0)$
$\boldsymbol{x}=\bigl(4,\tfrac{5}{2}\bigr)$

questions.question: Weak duality shows: if (P) $\max\{\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b},\ \boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ is unbounded, then its dual (D) $\min\{\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\colon\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{c},\ \boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ is infeasible. Which statement about the converse is correct?
options: If (D) is infeasible, then (P) is unbounded, because weak duality works in both directions.
If (D) is infeasible, then (P) is infeasible too, because infeasibility passes to the dual.
If (P) is infeasible, then (D) is unbounded, by running the same argument backwards.
If (D) is infeasible, (P) need not be unbounded, because both programs can be infeasible.

questions.question: Both (P) $\max\{\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b},\ \boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ and its dual (D) $\min\{\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\colon\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{c},\ \boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ have feasible solutions. Which argument shows that (P) has an optimal solution?
options: Weak duality bounds $Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ above, and a feasible linear program bounded above has an optimal solution.
Weak duality gives $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}$ for some feasible pair, and this common value is attained by (P).
Feasibility of (D) makes the feasible region of (P) bounded, so $Z$ attains a maximum on it.
The values of $Z$ are bounded above, and every set of reals bounded above contains its supremum.

questions.question: For the primal (P') $\min\{\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{b},\ \boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ and its dual (D') $\max\{\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\colon\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\leq\boldsymbol{c},\ \boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$, which inequality holds for every feasible pair $\boldsymbol{x}$, $\boldsymbol{y}$?
options: $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}$, since the primal value is always the smaller one.
$\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\leq\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$, since the maximization value is always the smaller one.
$\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\leq\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ only for optimal $\boldsymbol{x}$ and $\boldsymbol{y}$; other pairs can go either way.
No inequality in general, since weak duality needs the primal to be a maximization.

questions.question: For $\max Z=2x_1+3x_2$ subject to $x_1+2x_2\leq8$, $3x_1+x_2\leq9$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, the dual is $\min W=8y_1+9y_2$ subject to $y_1+3y_2\geq2$, $2y_1+y_2\geq3$, $\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$. Which candidate $\boldsymbol{y}$ proves, by weak duality, the smallest upper bound on $Z$ over the feasible region?
options: $\boldsymbol{y}=(1,1)$, bound $17$
$\boldsymbol{y}=\bigl(1,\tfrac{1}{2}\bigr)$, bound $\tfrac{25}{2}$
$\boldsymbol{y}=(2,0)$, bound $16$
$\boldsymbol{y}=(0,3)$, bound $27$

questions.question: For $\max Z=4x_1+3x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\leq5$, $2x_1+x_2\leq8$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, the point $\boldsymbol{x}=(3,2)$ is feasible with $Z=18$. The dual is $\min W=5y_1+8y_2$ subject to $y_1+2y_2\geq4$, $y_1+y_2\geq3$, $\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$. Which $\boldsymbol{y}$ proves, by weak duality, that $\boldsymbol{x}=(3,2)$ is optimal?
options: $\boldsymbol{y}=\bigl(0,\tfrac{9}{4}\bigr)$
$\boldsymbol{y}=\bigl(3,\tfrac{1}{2}\bigr)$
$\boldsymbol{y}=\bigl(1,\tfrac{3}{2}\bigr)$
$\boldsymbol{y}=(2,1)$

questions.question: For $\max Z=2x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\leq4$, $x_2\leq3$, $x_1,x_2\geq0$, the point $\boldsymbol{x}=(4,0)$ is feasible, and $\boldsymbol{y}=(2,-1)$ meets the dual constraints $y_1\geq2$, $y_1+y_2\geq1$ but has $y_2<0$. What happens to the chain $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\leq\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}$?
options: The second step fails: $\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}=8$ but $\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}=5$.
The first step fails: $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=8$ but $\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}=5$.
No step fails: $\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}=11$, so $8\leq8\leq11$ holds.
No step fails: $\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}=8$, so the chain is $8\leq8\leq8$.

questions.question: A feasible $\boldsymbol{x}$ of (P) $\max\{\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b},\ \boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ has objective value $20$; a feasible $\boldsymbol{y}$ of its dual (D) $\min\{\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\colon\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{c},\ \boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ has objective value $25$. Both have optimal values $Z^{\ast}$, $W^{\ast}$. Which statement about them is correct?
options: $\boldsymbol{x}$ is not optimal for (P), since an optimal solution of (P) would reach the value $25$.
$Z^{\ast}\leq25$ and $W^{\ast}\geq20$, and $\boldsymbol{x}$ may still be an optimal solution of (P).
$W^{\ast}-Z^{\ast}=5$, since the gap of this pair equals the gap between the optimal values.
$Z^{\ast}$ and $W^{\ast}$ both lie strictly between $20$ and $25$, since neither point is optimal.

questions.question: For feasible $\boldsymbol{x}$ of (P) $\max\{\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b},\ \boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ and $\boldsymbol{y}$ of its dual (D) $\min\{\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\colon\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{c},\ \boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$, weak duality is proved by the chain $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\leq\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}$. If its two outer values are equal, what holds for its two inequalities?
options: At least one of them is an equality, but the other one may still be strict.
Only the second must be an equality; the first is always an equality anyway.
Neither needs to be an equality; only the two outer values have to agree.
Both of them are equalities, so each of the two steps is tight.

questions.question: For $\max Z=x_1+\alpha x_2$ subject to $x_1-x_2\leq2$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, with a real parameter $\alpha$, the points $\boldsymbol{x}=(t+2,t)$, $t\geq0$, are feasible. For which $\alpha$ do these points show, by weak duality, that the dual $\min 2y$ subject to $y\geq1$, $-y\geq\alpha$, $y\geq0$ has no feasible solution?
options: Exactly for $\alpha>-1$
Exactly for $\alpha\geq-1$
Exactly for $\alpha<-1$
For every real $\alpha$, since the points form an unbounded set

questions.question: For $\max Z=2x_1+2x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\leq4$, $x_1\leq3$, $x_2\leq3$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, the point $\boldsymbol{x}=(2,2)$ is feasible but not a corner point, and $\boldsymbol{y}=(2,0,0)$ is feasible for the dual $\min W=4y_1+3y_2+3y_3$ subject to $y_1+y_2\geq2$, $y_1+y_3\geq2$, $\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$. Which conclusion is correct?
options: $\boldsymbol{x}$ is not optimal, since an optimum of a linear program is attained only at corner points.
$\boldsymbol{y}$ proves nothing, since its zero entries leave the constraints $x_1\leq3$, $x_2\leq3$ unused.
$\boldsymbol{x}$ is optimal, since $Z$ and $W$ both equal $8$ and weak duality then certifies optimality.
$\boldsymbol{x}$ is not shown optimal: that would also need $x_1\leq3$ and $x_2\leq3$ to be tight at $\boldsymbol{x}$.
